passages.title: Burnt offerings
passages.summary: The LORD speaks to Moses from the Tent of Meeting about offerings. A burnt offering from the herd must be a male without defect. The giver lays a hand on its head and kills it. The priests sprinkle its blood on the altar and arrange the pieces on the fire. The giver washes the inner parts and legs, and the priest burns all of it. The same steps apply to a sheep or goat. A burnt offering may also be doves or pigeons, which the priest handles. Each is called a pleasant aroma to the LORD.
passages.uncertainty: The marker represents the traditional Sinai region. Leviticus gives no chapter-by-chapter travel route.

lds.text: The giver lays a hand on the animal’s head (verse 4). What does the verse say the offering does for him?

contextNote.title: An offering divides work between the giver and the priests
contextNote.text: The chapter splits the work between two parties. The giver brings the animal, lays a hand on it, kills it, and washes it. The priests handle only the blood and the altar fire. Verse 4 ties the hand on its head to being “accepted for him.” So the offering is the giver’s own act, not a show he watches. A bull, a sheep, or a bird are all allowed (verses 3, 10, and 14). Each gets the same closing words: a pleasant aroma to the LORD.

passages.title: Grain offerings
passages.summary: A meal offering is fine flour with oil and frankincense. The priest burns a handful with all the frankincense as a memorial part. The rest belongs to Aaron and his sons and is most holy. The offering may be baked in an oven, on a griddle, or in a pan. It must have no yeast and no honey. Every meal offering must be seasoned with salt. A first fruits offering is fresh grain, roasted and crushed, with oil and frankincense.
passages.uncertainty: The marker represents the traditional Sinai region. Leviticus gives no chapter-by-chapter travel route.

lds.text: Only a handful of the flour is burned (verse 2). Who receives the rest in verse 3?

contextNote.title: An ordinary food gift also supports sacred work
contextNote.text: Flour, oil, and salt are kitchen goods, not herd animals. So this offering comes from daily bread. Verse 2 has the priest burn only a handful. Verse 3 gives the rest to Aaron and his sons. The gift to God is also the priests’ food, and it is called “most holy.” Priests had no fields of their own to harvest (Numbers 18:20–21). So a household’s bread helped keep the tent’s workers fed.

passages.title: Fellowship offerings
passages.summary: A peace offering may be a male or female animal without defect. It may come from the herd, the sheep, or the goats. The giver lays a hand on its head and kills it at the tent door. The priests sprinkle the blood around the altar. The fat around the inner parts, the kidneys, and the liver cover are burned. For a lamb, the whole fat tail is burned too. All the fat belongs to the LORD. Israel must never eat fat or blood.
passages.uncertainty: The marker represents the traditional Sinai region. Leviticus gives no chapter-by-chapter travel route.

lds.text: The peace offering ends with a rule for every home (verse 17). What two things may Israel never eat?

contextNote.title: A shared offering still places limits on consumption
contextNote.text: Chapter 7:15 shows that the giver ate meat from a peace offering. So this is a shared meal, unlike the burnt offering of chapter 1. Chapter 3 says what is held back from the table. The fat is burned, and verse 16 says, “all the fat is the LORD’s.” The blood goes on the altar. Verse 17 turns that into a lasting rule “in all your dwellings.” Even a feast with God keeps some parts that are not for the eater.

passages.title: Offerings for unintentional sin
passages.summary: These offerings are for sins done without meaning to. If the anointed priest sins, the people share the guilt, and he offers a bull. Its blood is sprinkled before the veil, and its body is burned outside the camp. If the whole assembly sins, the elders lay hands on a bull. A ruler who sins brings a male goat. A common person brings a female goat or lamb. In each case the priest makes atonement, and the person is forgiven.
passages.uncertainty: The marker represents the traditional Sinai region. Leviticus gives no chapter-by-chapter travel route.

lds.text: The priest’s sin brings guilt “on the people” (verse 3). How does his offering compare with a common person’s in verse 28?

contextNote.title: An error by a leader can involve a wider community
contextNote.text: The chapter sorts offerings by who sinned. A priest or the whole assembly brings a bull (verses 3 and 14). A ruler brings a male goat, and a common person a female goat or lamb. The size of the animal follows the reach of the person’s role. Verse 3 says why: the priest’s sin brings guilt on the people. For priest and assembly the blood is taken inside the tent (verses 6 and 17). The assembly, ruler, and common person each end forgiven (verses 20, 26, 31).

passages.title: Confession and repair
passages.summary: Some cases need a trespass offering. A witness stays silent, a person touches something unclean, or someone swears a rash oath. The guilty person must confess the sin. He brings a female lamb or goat, and the priest makes atonement. If he cannot afford a lamb, he brings two doves or pigeons. If he cannot afford birds, he brings a tenth of an ephah of flour. One who misuses holy things brings a ram, repays the loss, and adds a fifth. A person who sins without knowing it is still guilty and brings a ram.
passages.uncertainty: The marker represents the traditional Sinai region. Leviticus gives no chapter-by-chapter travel route.

lds.text: Someone who cannot afford a lamb may bring birds or flour (verses 7, 11). What does the priest still do for him in verse 13?

contextNote.title: Access to worship includes those with less
contextNote.text: Verse 6 sets the normal offering at a lamb or goat. Verse 7 opens a second door for someone who “can’t afford a lamb.” Verse 11 opens a third: a small measure of flour. Each level ends with the same words: atonement, and “he will be forgiven.” So the price changes with the person’s means, and the result does not. Verse 5 asks one thing of everyone first: to confess. Verse 16 adds repayment plus a fifth where something was taken.

passages.title: Restitution and priestly duties
passages.summary: A person may cheat a neighbor over a deposit, a theft, or a found item. He must return it in full and add a fifth. He gives it to the owner on the day he is found guilty. Then he brings a ram as a trespass offering and is forgiven. The priests must keep the altar fire burning all night and clear the ashes. The priests eat what is left of the meal offering in a holy place. A priest’s own meal offering is burned whole. The priest who offers a sin offering eats it in the court.
passages.uncertainty: The marker represents the traditional Sinai region. Leviticus gives no chapter-by-chapter travel route.

lds.text: The wrongdoer pays the neighbor back and adds a fifth (verse 5). Which comes first in verses 5–6, the repayment or the offering?

contextNote.title: Repair reaches the person whose property was taken
contextNote.text: Verse 2 calls cheating a neighbor “a trespass against the LORD.” So a wrong against a person is also a wrong against God. Verse 5 deals with the person first. The item goes back in full, plus a fifth, to “him to whom it belongs.” It must happen the day guilt is found, not later. Only then does verse 6 bring the ram to the priest. Forgiveness in verse 7 follows repair, and does not replace it.

passages.title: Rules for shared offerings
passages.summary: The trespass offering is most holy, and the priests eat it in a holy place. The priest who offers a burnt offering keeps its skin. A peace offering for thanksgiving comes with cakes and bread. Its meat must be eaten the same day. Meat from a vow or free will offering may be eaten for two days. Anything left on the third day is burned. No one may eat fat or blood, and the unclean may not eat this meat. The breast and right thigh of peace offerings go to the priests.
passages.uncertainty: The marker represents the traditional Sinai region. Leviticus gives no chapter-by-chapter travel route.

lds.text: Thanksgiving meat must be eaten that day (verse 15). What does that rule do with a whole animal’s worth of food?

contextNote.title: A thanksgiving offering creates food that cannot be kept indefinitely
contextNote.text: A whole animal is more meat than one family can eat in a day. Verse 15 says none of the thanksgiving meat may be left until morning. So the giver would need others to help eat it. The meat cannot be stored up as private stock. Verses 16–18 allow one more day for vows and free gifts, then require burning. Verse 14 gives a share of the bread to the priest. Thanks to God is shown here by a table that others eat from.

passages.title: Priests appointed
passages.summary: The LORD tells Moses to gather all the people at the tent door. Moses washes Aaron and his sons before them. He dresses Aaron in the tunic, robe, ephod, breastplate, and turban. He anoints the tabernacle, the altar, and Aaron with oil. He offers a bull for sin and a ram as a burnt offering. He puts blood from a second ram on their right ears, thumbs, and big toes. He sprinkles oil and blood on them and their garments. They stay at the tent door seven days.
passages.uncertainty: The marker represents the traditional Sinai region. Leviticus gives no chapter-by-chapter travel route.

lds.text: The Church manual connects priestly service with sacred preparation. Who is called to watch Aaron’s appointment (verses 3–4)?

contextNote.title: The community witnesses the beginning of priestly authority
contextNote.text: Exodus 29 gave these steps as orders. Here Moses carries them out one by one. Verse 3 adds where: in front of “all the congregation.” The people see Aaron washed, dressed, and anointed. So his office is not a private claim. Everyone knows who made him priest and how. The phrase “as the LORD commanded Moses” keeps returning (verses 9, 13, 17, 21, 29).

passages.title: The first priestly service
passages.summary: On the eighth day Moses tells Aaron to offer a calf for his own sin. The people bring a goat, a calf, a lamb, a bull, and a ram. Moses says the LORD’s glory will appear to them. Aaron first offers the sin offering and burnt offering for himself. Then he offers the people’s goat, burnt offering, meal offering, and peace offerings. He lifts his hands and blesses the people. Moses and Aaron go into the tent, come out, and bless them again. The LORD’s glory appears, fire burns the offering, and the people fall down.
passages.uncertainty: The marker represents the traditional Sinai region. Leviticus gives no chapter-by-chapter travel route.

lds.text: Aaron must make atonement “for yourself, and for the people” (verse 7). Whose offering does he make first in verse 8?

contextNote.title: The priest must address his own need before serving others
contextNote.text: Verse 7 gives the order: his own sin offering first, then the people’s. Verse 8 says the calf “was for himself.” Aaron made the gold calf in Exodus 32:4. His first offering is a calf. The priest stands with the people as someone who also needs atonement. Only after both offerings does he bless them (verse 22). The fire in verse 24 shows the offerings were accepted.

passages.title: Nadab and Abihu die
passages.summary: Aaron’s sons Nadab and Abihu offer strange fire that the LORD did not command. Fire comes out from the LORD and kills them. Moses says God will be shown holy, and Aaron keeps silent. Cousins carry the bodies out of the camp. Aaron and his other sons may not mourn openly or leave the tent. The LORD tells Aaron that priests must not drink wine on duty. They must tell holy from common and teach Israel the laws. Moses is angry that the sin offering was burned, not eaten, and accepts Aaron’s answer.
passages.uncertainty: The marker represents the traditional Sinai region. Leviticus gives no chapter-by-chapter travel route.

lds.text: The Church manual discusses responsibility in sacred service. Aaron explains why he did not eat the offering (verse 19). How does Moses respond in verse 20?

contextNote.title: Grief creates a question within the prescribed service
contextNote.text: Aaron has lost two sons that day and may not mourn (verses 6–7). The rule was that priests eat the sin offering (6:26). Aaron’s remaining sons burned it, and Moses is angry (verses 16–18). Aaron answers with a question in verse 19. After “such things as these,” would eating it have pleased the LORD? He does not claim a rule; he asks what fits the day. Verse 20 says Moses was satisfied, and the chapter ends there.

passages.title: Animals and food
passages.summary: The LORD tells Moses and Aaron which animals Israel may eat. Land animals must have a split hoof and chew the cud. Camels, hyraxes, hares, and pigs are unclean. Water creatures must have fins and scales. Many named birds are forbidden, and so are most winged insects, except locusts and grasshoppers. Touching a dead unclean animal makes a person unclean until evening. Pots and ovens that touch a carcass must be washed or broken. Israel must be holy, because the LORD who brought them from Egypt is holy.
passages.uncertainty: The marker represents the traditional Sinai region. Leviticus gives no chapter-by-chapter travel route.

lds.text: The Church manual studies these rules within Israel’s covenant. A person who carries a carcass is unclean “until the evening” (verse 40). What must that person do?

contextNote.title: Temporary uncleanness requires a process rather than a moral verdict
contextNote.text: Verse 40 is about an animal Israel may eat that dies by itself. Someone has to move the body. The verse does not forbid it or call it sin. It says to wash clothes and wait until evening. So “unclean” here is a short state with a simple way out. It limits contact with holy things for a time. Verses 44–45 give the reason for the rules: “be holy; for I am holy.”

passages.title: After childbirth
passages.summary: A woman who bears a son is unclean for seven days. The boy is circumcised on the eighth day. She then waits thirty-three more days and may not enter the sanctuary. For a daughter the times are doubled: two weeks and sixty-six days. When the time ends, she brings the priest a lamb and a pigeon or dove. If she cannot afford a lamb, she brings two doves or two pigeons. The priest makes atonement for her, and she is clean.
passages.uncertainty: The marker represents the traditional Sinai region. Leviticus gives no chapter-by-chapter travel route.

lds.text: A mother who cannot afford a lamb may bring two birds (verse 8). What result does the verse promise her?

contextNote.title: Childbirth rules govern access without accusing the mother of a crime
contextNote.text: The chapter does not say the mother did wrong. Genesis 1:28 commands people to be fruitful. Her state comes from the blood of birth, as verses 4 and 7 say. It keeps her from holy things and the sanctuary for a set time. Verse 8 lowers the cost for a poor family, as 5:7 did. The result is the same either way: “she shall be clean.” Luke 2:22–24 reports that Mary brought the two birds.

passages.title: Inspection of skin and cloth
passages.summary: A person with a swelling, scab, or bright spot goes to a priest. The priest looks for white hair and a mark deeper than the skin. If it is unclear, he isolates the person for seven days and looks again. He may wait seven more days before deciding. A faded mark means clean, and a spreading one means unclean. A person with leprosy wears torn clothes, calls out “Unclean,” and lives outside the camp. Cloth or leather with a greenish or reddish spot is also shown to the priest. It is shut away seven days and burned if the spot spreads.
passages.uncertainty: The marker represents the traditional Sinai region. Leviticus gives no chapter-by-chapter travel route.

lds.text: The priest waits seven days, then seven more, before he decides (verses 4–5). How can a community care for people who must stay apart?

contextNote.title: Inspection makes time part of the decision
contextNote.text: The priest here works as an inspector, and the chapter gives him tests. He checks hair color, depth, and spread (verses 3–8). When the signs are unclear, verse 4 orders a seven-day wait. Verse 5 orders a second look and, if needed, a second wait. So no one is sent out of the camp on a first glance. Verse 46 shows why care matters: the unclean person must live alone outside.

passages.title: Return after cleansing
passages.summary: This is the law for a healed leper. The priest goes outside the camp to examine him. Two birds are used: one is killed, and the living one is set free. The person washes, shaves, and waits seven days before entering his tent. On the eighth day he brings lambs, flour, and oil, and the priest makes atonement. A poor person may bring one lamb and two birds. A house with spreading mildew is emptied, shut up, scraped, and, if needed, torn down. A house that stays clear is declared clean.
passages.uncertainty: The marker represents the traditional Sinai region. Leviticus gives no chapter-by-chapter travel route.

lds.text: A poor person brings “such as he is able to afford” (verse 22). How does the chapter help someone return to the community?

contextNote.title: Return from separation includes provision for limited means
contextNote.text: Chapter 13 sent the sick person outside the camp. Chapter 14 is about the way back. The priest goes out to meet him (verse 3). The return happens in steps: outside, into the camp, into the tent, to the altar. Verse 21 makes sure cost does not block the last step. A poor person brings one lamb, not three, and two birds. The closing words are the same for rich and poor: “he shall be clean.”

passages.title: Bodily discharges
passages.summary: A man with a bodily discharge is unclean. His bed, his seat, and anyone he touches become unclean until evening. When it stops, he counts seven days, washes, and brings two birds to the priest. A man with an emission of semen bathes and is unclean until evening. A woman in her monthly period is unclean for seven days. A longer flow of blood makes her unclean for as long as it lasts. When it stops, she counts seven days and brings two birds. These rules keep Israel from defiling the tabernacle that is among them.
passages.uncertainty: The marker represents the traditional Sinai region. Leviticus gives no chapter-by-chapter travel route.

lds.text: Verse 31 gives the reason for these rules. What is it?

contextNote.title: Ordinary bodily conditions affect access to sacred space
contextNote.text: The chapter covers things that happen to healthy bodies and to sick ones. It treats men first (verses 2–18) and women second (verses 19–30). Most cases need only washing and waiting until evening. None is called a crime. Verse 31 gives the reason for all of it: God’s tabernacle is “among them.” Because he lives in the camp, the people’s bodily states matter near his tent. The rules manage access to that tent and say nothing about a person’s worth.

passages.title: The Day of Atonement
passages.summary: Aaron may not enter the Most Holy Place at just any time. Once a year he bathes and dresses in plain linen. He offers a bull for himself and his house. He casts lots over two goats: one for the LORD and one as the scapegoat. He takes incense and blood inside the veil and sprinkles the mercy seat. He makes atonement for the Holy Place, the tent, and the altar. He confesses Israel’s sins over the live goat and sends it into the wilderness. On that day, the tenth of the seventh month, all Israel rests and humbles itself.
passages.uncertainty: The marker represents the traditional Sinai region. Leviticus gives no chapter-by-chapter travel route.

lds.text: The older Church manual connects the Day of Atonement with Christ’s work to forgive sin. Verse 16 says the tent dwells “in the middle of their uncleanness.” What is cleansed on this day besides the people?

contextNote.title: The annual rite addresses the sanctuary as well as the people
contextNote.text: Verse 16 says atonement is made “for the Holy Place.” The reason is the people’s uncleanness and all their sins. The tent stands in the middle of the camp, so their wrongs reach it. Once a year the room, the tent, and the altar are cleansed (verse 20). Then the people’s sins are confessed over a goat and carried away (verses 21–22). The day clears both the place and the people. Verse 30 states the result: “You shall be clean from all your sins.”

passages.title: Blood and the place of offering
passages.summary: Anyone who kills a bull, lamb, or goat must bring it to the tent door. Killing it elsewhere counts as bloodshed. The rule is meant to end sacrifices in the open field to goat idols. The priest sprinkles the blood on the LORD’s altar. No Israelite or foreigner living among them may eat blood. The life is in the blood, and God gave it for atonement on the altar. A hunter must pour out the blood of his catch and cover it with dust. Anyone who eats an animal found dead must wash and wait until evening.
passages.uncertainty: The marker represents the traditional Sinai region. Leviticus gives no chapter-by-chapter travel route.

lds.text: Verse 11 says “the life of the flesh is in the blood.” What must a hunter do with an animal’s blood in verse 13?

contextNote.title: Blood receives a stated meaning within the ritual system
contextNote.text: The ban on eating blood appeared in Genesis 9:4 and Leviticus 3:17. Verse 11 is where the reason is given. Blood stands for the animal’s life. God says he has “given it to you on the altar” for atonement. So blood has one proper use, and it is not food. Verse 13 applies this even to wild game that is never offered. The hunter pours the blood out and covers it, treating the life with respect.

passages.title: Limits on sexual conduct
passages.summary: The LORD tells Israel not to follow the practices of Egypt or Canaan. They must keep his statutes and live by them. The chapter forbids sexual relations with close relatives, and it lists them one by one. It forbids marrying a wife’s sister as a rival, and adultery. It forbids giving children to Molech. It forbids a man lying with a man, and sex with animals. The nations before Israel did these things, and the land was defiled. The land vomited them out, and it will do the same to Israel.
passages.uncertainty: The marker represents the traditional Sinai region. Leviticus gives no chapter-by-chapter travel route.

lds.text: Verse 28 warns that the land can “vomit you out also.” Whom do the rules in verses 6–18 protect inside a household?

contextNote.title: The land becomes part of the warning about conduct
contextNote.text: Most of the chapter concerns people who live in one large household. Verses 6–18 name mothers, sisters, granddaughters, aunts, and daughters-in-law. Each rule is addressed to the one who would approach, so the relative is protected. Verses 24–25 widen the view to the land itself. Canaan’s people defiled it, and it “vomited out her inhabitants.” Verse 28 gives Israel the same warning, with no special protection.

passages.title: Holiness in daily life
passages.summary: The LORD tells all Israel to be holy, because he is holy. They must respect parents, keep Sabbaths, and avoid idols. Farmers must leave field corners and fallen grapes for the poor and the foreigner. They must not steal, lie, hold back wages overnight, or trip the blind. Judges must not favor the poor or the great. They must not hate or take revenge, but love their neighbor as themselves. They must love the foreigner as themselves, since they were foreigners in Egypt. Scales, weights, and measures must be honest.
passages.uncertainty: The marker represents the traditional Sinai region. Leviticus gives no chapter-by-chapter travel route.

lds.text: How can love change the way you treat workers and strangers? Verse 36 requires honest weights. What does verse 13 require for a hired worker’s pay?

contextNote.title: Holiness reaches the marketplace
contextNote.text: The chapter opens with “You shall be holy” (verse 2). It then spends most of its length on fields, wages, courts, and trade. Verse 36 ends the list at the scale: just balances, weights, and measures. A false weight cheats a buyer; the trade weight shown is that kind of tool. The verse ends with the exodus: “who brought you out of the land of Egypt.” So honest trade is part of belonging to the God who freed them. The same chapter holds “love your neighbor as yourself” (verse 18).

passages.title: Penalties and distinction
passages.summary: Anyone who gives a child to Molech must be stoned. If the people look away, God will act against that family. Those who turn to mediums are cut off. Israel must be holy and keep God’s statutes. Death is set for cursing parents, adultery, and several unions forbidden in chapter 18. Other unions bring being cut off or dying childless. Israel must not follow the customs of the nations being driven out. The LORD has set them apart to be his and to inherit the land.
passages.uncertainty: The marker represents the traditional Sinai region. Leviticus gives no chapter-by-chapter travel route.

lds.text: Consider moral responsibility while keeping ancient civil penalties distinct from present Church practice. The LORD says he has “separated you from the peoples” (verse 24). What promise comes with that in the same verse?

contextNote.title: Distinct identity comes with threats of exclusion and death
contextNote.text: Chapter 18 listed forbidden acts. Chapter 20 attaches penalties, and many are death. Verses 2–5 begin with child sacrifice to Molech and blame neighbors who look away. Verses 22–23 give the reason: other nations did these things and lost the land. Verse 24 sets the promise beside the threat. Israel will inherit a good land and has been separated from the peoples. Verse 26 says what the separation is for: “that you should be mine.”

passages.title: Rules for priests
passages.summary: Priests may not touch the dead, except for their closest relatives. They may not shave their heads or cut their flesh. They may not marry a prostitute or a divorced woman. The high priest may not go near any dead body, even a parent’s. He must marry a virgin of his own people. A priest with a bodily defect may not come near the altar or the veil. The list includes the blind, the lame, and the injured. He may still eat the holy and most holy food.
passages.uncertainty: The marker represents the traditional Sinai region. Leviticus gives no chapter-by-chapter travel route.

lds.text: What duties come with service in a holy place? A priest with a defect may not serve at the altar (verse 21). What does verse 22 still give him?

contextNote.title: A limit on priestly service does not remove every priestly share
contextNote.text: Verses 17–21 bar a priest with a bodily defect from offering at the altar. The same standard was set for the animals offered there (1:3). Verse 22 follows at once with what he keeps. He eats “the bread of his God,” both the holy and the most holy. That food was the priests’ living (6:16–18). So the limit is on one task, not on his place among the priests. The text does not call him unclean or sinful.

passages.title: Holy gifts and acceptable offerings
passages.summary: Priests must stay away from the holy food while they are unclean. An unclean priest washes, waits until evening, and then may eat his bread. Only the priest’s household may eat it, including a slave he bought. A married daughter may not, but a childless widow who returns home may. Anyone who eats it by mistake repays it and adds a fifth. Animals for vows and free gifts must have no defect. A newborn animal stays seven days with its mother. A cow or ewe and its young may not be killed on the same day.
passages.uncertainty: The marker represents the traditional Sinai region. Leviticus gives no chapter-by-chapter travel route.

lds.text: An animal and its young may not be killed on one day (verse 28). What does verse 27 require for a newborn animal?

contextNote.title: An offering rule also limits how an animal family is treated
contextNote.text: Most of this chapter is about what makes an offering acceptable. Verses 27–28 add two limits that concern the animals themselves. A newborn stays with its mother for seven days. A mother and her young are not killed on the same day. The text gives no reason. The effect is to keep mother and young in view. Even at the altar, the animal’s life is given some regard.

passages.title: The sacred calendar
passages.summary: The LORD gives Moses the set feasts of the year. The Sabbath comes every seventh day. Passover falls in the first month, with seven days of unleavened bread. A sheaf of first grain is waved, and fifty days later two loaves are offered. At harvest the field corners and gleanings are left for the poor and the foreigner. The seventh month has a day of trumpets and the day of atonement. Then comes the seven-day feast of booths. Israel lives in shelters to remember the journey out of Egypt.
passages.uncertainty: The marker represents the traditional Sinai region. Leviticus gives no chapter-by-chapter travel route.

lds.text: A harvest rule sits in the middle of the feast list (verse 22). Whom does it provide for?

contextNote.title: The festival calendar includes people without their own harvest
contextNote.text: Verses 4–21 and 23–44 are a calendar of feasts and offerings. Verse 22 interrupts it with a rule about reaping. It comes right after the harvest feast of verses 15–21. The farmer who brings loaves to God must leave grain in the field. The poor and the foreigner have no harvest of their own to celebrate. The rule repeats 19:9–10 almost word for word. So the feast is not complete if the harvest is kept only for the owner.

passages.title: Lamps, bread, and a judgment
passages.summary: Israel must bring pure olive oil so the lamp burns every night. Twelve loaves are set on the gold table each Sabbath, and the priests eat them. Then a fight breaks out in the camp. A man with an Israelite mother and an Egyptian father curses the Name. He is held until the LORD’s will is known. The LORD orders the hearers to lay hands on him and all to stone him. The LORD adds rules: life for life, eye for eye, and payment for animals. The same law applies to the foreigner and the native-born.
passages.uncertainty: The marker represents the traditional Sinai region. Leviticus gives no chapter-by-chapter travel route.

lds.text: How can our words honor God? Verse 22 says one law covers the foreigner and the native-born. Why does that matter in this case (verses 10–11)?

contextNote.title: A single legal standard stands beside a severe public judgment
contextNote.text: The man in this case has an Egyptian father (verse 10). The people wait for the LORD’s word before acting (verse 12). The ruling does not rest on his mixed family. Verse 16 says a foreigner or a native-born person gets the same penalty. Verse 22 states it as a rule: “one kind of law” for both. The same verses limit payback to the harm done: eye for eye, no more. The sentence is severe, and the text reports that it was carried out (verse 23).

passages.title: Sabbath years and Jubilee
passages.summary: Every seventh year the land must rest, with no sowing or pruning. After forty-nine years a trumpet announces the fiftieth year, the Jubilee. Liberty is declared, and each person returns to his family’s land. Land prices follow the number of crops left before the Jubilee. The land may not be sold forever, because it belongs to the LORD. A relative may buy back land for a poor brother. Israel must lend to the poor without interest. A poor Israelite who sells himself serves as hired help until the Jubilee.
passages.uncertainty: The marker represents the traditional Sinai region. Leviticus gives no chapter-by-chapter travel route.

lds.text: The LORD says, “The land is mine” (verse 23). What does that mean for a family that had to sell its field?

contextNote.title: Land ownership has limits
contextNote.text: Verse 23 gives the reason behind the whole chapter. The land belongs to the LORD, and Israel lives on it as his guests. So a sale is really a lease of crops until the Jubilee (verses 15–16). A family that falls into debt gets its field back in the fiftieth year. Verse 42 says the same of people: Israelites are God’s servants, not slaves. The chapter does not extend that rule to foreigners (verses 44–46). Its limit on wealth protects Israel’s own families from permanent loss.

passages.title: Covenant promises and warnings
passages.summary: Israel must make no idols and must keep the Sabbaths. If they obey, God will send rain, harvests, peace, and victory. He will set his tent among them and walk with them. If they refuse, he will send sickness, defeat, drought, wild animals, and siege. Each stage is harder than the last. In the end their cities fall, and they are scattered among the nations. Then the land will enjoy the Sabbaths it missed. If they confess, God will remember his covenant with Jacob, Isaac, and Abraham.
passages.uncertainty: The marker represents the traditional Sinai region. Leviticus gives no chapter-by-chapter travel route.

lds.text: What hope remains after the warnings? In verse 44 God says he will not reject his people in exile. What will he remember in verse 45?

contextNote.title: The warnings do not end with rejection in exile
contextNote.text: The warnings come in five stages (verses 16, 18, 21, 23, 27). Each stage is a chance to turn back before the next. The last stage is exile in an enemy’s land. Verse 44 begins “Yet for all that.” Even there God will not destroy them utterly or break his covenant. The reason given is his name: “for I am the LORD their God.” Verses 40–42 say what opens the way back: confession and a humbled heart.

passages.title: Vows and dedicated property
passages.summary: A person vowed to the LORD is given a value in silver. The value depends on age and sex, from three to fifty shekels. A poor person is valued by the priest according to what he can pay. An animal given for offering becomes holy and may not be swapped. A house or field may be dedicated and bought back by adding a fifth. A field’s value is counted by the years left until the Jubilee. Firstborn animals already belong to the LORD. A tenth of crops and herds is holy to the LORD.
passages.uncertainty: The marker represents the traditional Sinai region. Leviticus gives no chapter-by-chapter travel route.

lds.text: A person too poor for the set value goes to the priest (verse 8). How does the priest decide the amount?

contextNote.title: A vow requires rules for people who cannot meet the valuation
contextNote.text: Verses 3–7 set fixed values for people who have been vowed. A fixed scale is simple, but it can be out of reach. Verse 8 handles that case. The priest sets a value “according to his ability to pay.” So a vow made in faith does not become a debt that crushes. The same care appeared in 5:7, 12:8, and 14:21. Leviticus ends as it began, making room for people with less.

events.title: Burnt offerings
events.summary: The LORD speaks to Moses from the Tent of Meeting about offerings. A burnt offering from the herd must be a male without defect. The giver lays a hand on its head and kills it. The priests sprinkle its blood on the altar and arrange the pieces on the fire. The giver washes the inner parts and legs, and the priest burns all of it. The same steps apply to a sheep or goat. A burnt offering may also be doves or pigeons, which the priest handles. Each is called a pleasant aroma to the LORD.
events.detail: The chapter splits the work between two parties. The giver brings the animal, lays a hand on it, kills it, and washes it. The priests handle only the blood and the altar fire. Verse 4 ties the hand on its head to being “accepted for him.” So the offering is the giver’s own act, not a show he watches. A bull, a sheep, or a bird are all allowed (verses 3, 10, and 14). Each gets the same closing words: a pleasant aroma to the LORD.
events.uncertainty: The marker represents the traditional Sinai region. Leviticus gives no chapter-by-chapter travel route.

lds.text: The giver lays a hand on the animal’s head (verse 4). What does the verse say the offering does for him?

events.title: Grain offerings
events.summary: A meal offering is fine flour with oil and frankincense. The priest burns a handful with all the frankincense as a memorial part. The rest belongs to Aaron and his sons and is most holy. The offering may be baked in an oven, on a griddle, or in a pan. It must have no yeast and no honey. Every meal offering must be seasoned with salt. A first fruits offering is fresh grain, roasted and crushed, with oil and frankincense.
events.detail: Flour, oil, and salt are kitchen goods, not herd animals. So this offering comes from daily bread. Verse 2 has the priest burn only a handful. Verse 3 gives the rest to Aaron and his sons. The gift to God is also the priests’ food, and it is called “most holy.” Priests had no fields of their own to harvest (Numbers 18:20–21). So a household’s bread helped keep the tent’s workers fed.
events.uncertainty: The marker represents the traditional Sinai region. Leviticus gives no chapter-by-chapter travel route.

lds.text: Only a handful of the flour is burned (verse 2). Who receives the rest in verse 3?

events.title: Fellowship offerings
events.summary: A peace offering may be a male or female animal without defect. It may come from the herd, the sheep, or the goats. The giver lays a hand on its head and kills it at the tent door. The priests sprinkle the blood around the altar. The fat around the inner parts, the kidneys, and the liver cover are burned. For a lamb, the whole fat tail is burned too. All the fat belongs to the LORD. Israel must never eat fat or blood.
events.detail: Chapter 7:15 shows that the giver ate meat from a peace offering. So this is a shared meal, unlike the burnt offering of chapter 1. Chapter 3 says what is held back from the table. The fat is burned, and verse 16 says, “all the fat is the LORD’s.” The blood goes on the altar. Verse 17 turns that into a lasting rule “in all your dwellings.” Even a feast with God keeps some parts that are not for the eater.
events.uncertainty: The marker represents the traditional Sinai region. Leviticus gives no chapter-by-chapter travel route.

lds.text: The peace offering ends with a rule for every home (verse 17). What two things may Israel never eat?

events.title: Offerings for unintentional sin
events.summary: These offerings are for sins done without meaning to. If the anointed priest sins, the people share the guilt, and he offers a bull. Its blood is sprinkled before the veil, and its body is burned outside the camp. If the whole assembly sins, the elders lay hands on a bull. A ruler who sins brings a male goat. A common person brings a female goat or lamb. In each case the priest makes atonement, and the person is forgiven.
events.detail: The chapter sorts offerings by who sinned. A priest or the whole assembly brings a bull (verses 3 and 14). A ruler brings a male goat, and a common person a female goat or lamb. The size of the animal follows the reach of the person’s role. Verse 3 says why: the priest’s sin brings guilt on the people. For priest and assembly the blood is taken inside the tent (verses 6 and 17). The assembly, ruler, and common person each end forgiven (verses 20, 26, 31).
events.uncertainty: The marker represents the traditional Sinai region. Leviticus gives no chapter-by-chapter travel route.

lds.text: The priest’s sin brings guilt “on the people” (verse 3). How does his offering compare with a common person’s in verse 28?

events.title: Confession and repair
events.summary: Some cases need a trespass offering. A witness stays silent, a person touches something unclean, or someone swears a rash oath. The guilty person must confess the sin. He brings a female lamb or goat, and the priest makes atonement. If he cannot afford a lamb, he brings two doves or pigeons. If he cannot afford birds, he brings a tenth of an ephah of flour. One who misuses holy things brings a ram, repays the loss, and adds a fifth. A person who sins without knowing it is still guilty and brings a ram.
events.detail: Verse 6 sets the normal offering at a lamb or goat. Verse 7 opens a second door for someone who “can’t afford a lamb.” Verse 11 opens a third: a small measure of flour. Each level ends with the same words: atonement, and “he will be forgiven.” So the price changes with the person’s means, and the result does not. Verse 5 asks one thing of everyone first: to confess. Verse 16 adds repayment plus a fifth where something was taken.
events.uncertainty: The marker represents the traditional Sinai region. Leviticus gives no chapter-by-chapter travel route.

lds.text: Someone who cannot afford a lamb may bring birds or flour (verses 7, 11). What does the priest still do for him in verse 13?

events.title: Restitution and priestly duties
events.summary: A person may cheat a neighbor over a deposit, a theft, or a found item. He must return it in full and add a fifth. He gives it to the owner on the day he is found guilty. Then he brings a ram as a trespass offering and is forgiven. The priests must keep the altar fire burning all night and clear the ashes. The priests eat what is left of the meal offering in a holy place. A priest’s own meal offering is burned whole. The priest who offers a sin offering eats it in the court.
events.detail: Verse 2 calls cheating a neighbor “a trespass against the LORD.” So a wrong against a person is also a wrong against God. Verse 5 deals with the person first. The item goes back in full, plus a fifth, to “him to whom it belongs.” It must happen the day guilt is found, not later. Only then does verse 6 bring the ram to the priest. Forgiveness in verse 7 follows repair, and does not replace it.
events.uncertainty: The marker represents the traditional Sinai region. Leviticus gives no chapter-by-chapter travel route.

lds.text: The wrongdoer pays the neighbor back and adds a fifth (verse 5). Which comes first in verses 5–6, the repayment or the offering?

events.title: Rules for shared offerings
events.summary: The trespass offering is most holy, and the priests eat it in a holy place. The priest who offers a burnt offering keeps its skin. A peace offering for thanksgiving comes with cakes and bread. Its meat must be eaten the same day. Meat from a vow or free will offering may be eaten for two days. Anything left on the third day is burned. No one may eat fat or blood, and the unclean may not eat this meat. The breast and right thigh of peace offerings go to the priests.
events.detail: A whole animal is more meat than one family can eat in a day. Verse 15 says none of the thanksgiving meat may be left until morning. So the giver would need others to help eat it. The meat cannot be stored up as private stock. Verses 16–18 allow one more day for vows and free gifts, then require burning. Verse 14 gives a share of the bread to the priest. Thanks to God is shown here by a table that others eat from.
events.uncertainty: The marker represents the traditional Sinai region. Leviticus gives no chapter-by-chapter travel route.

lds.text: Thanksgiving meat must be eaten that day (verse 15). What does that rule do with a whole animal’s worth of food?

events.title: Priests appointed
events.summary: The LORD tells Moses to gather all the people at the tent door. Moses washes Aaron and his sons before them. He dresses Aaron in the tunic, robe, ephod, breastplate, and turban. He anoints the tabernacle, the altar, and Aaron with oil. He offers a bull for sin and a ram as a burnt offering. He puts blood from a second ram on their right ears, thumbs, and big toes. He sprinkles oil and blood on them and their garments. They stay at the tent door seven days.
events.detail: Exodus 29 gave these steps as orders. Here Moses carries them out one by one. Verse 3 adds where: in front of “all the congregation.” The people see Aaron washed, dressed, and anointed. So his office is not a private claim. Everyone knows who made him priest and how. The phrase “as the LORD commanded Moses” keeps returning (verses 9, 13, 17, 21, 29).
events.uncertainty: The marker represents the traditional Sinai region. Leviticus gives no chapter-by-chapter travel route.

lds.text: The Church manual connects priestly service with sacred preparation. Who is called to watch Aaron’s appointment (verses 3–4)?

events.title: The first priestly service
events.summary: On the eighth day Moses tells Aaron to offer a calf for his own sin. The people bring a goat, a calf, a lamb, a bull, and a ram. Moses says the LORD’s glory will appear to them. Aaron first offers the sin offering and burnt offering for himself. Then he offers the people’s goat, burnt offering, meal offering, and peace offerings. He lifts his hands and blesses the people. Moses and Aaron go into the tent, come out, and bless them again. The LORD’s glory appears, fire burns the offering, and the people fall down.
events.detail: Verse 7 gives the order: his own sin offering first, then the people’s. Verse 8 says the calf “was for himself.” Aaron made the gold calf in Exodus 32:4. His first offering is a calf. The priest stands with the people as someone who also needs atonement. Only after both offerings does he bless them (verse 22). The fire in verse 24 shows the offerings were accepted.
events.uncertainty: The marker represents the traditional Sinai region. Leviticus gives no chapter-by-chapter travel route.

lds.text: Aaron must make atonement “for yourself, and for the people” (verse 7). Whose offering does he make first in verse 8?

events.title: Nadab and Abihu die
events.summary: Aaron’s sons Nadab and Abihu offer strange fire that the LORD did not command. Fire comes out from the LORD and kills them. Moses says God will be shown holy, and Aaron keeps silent. Cousins carry the bodies out of the camp. Aaron and his other sons may not mourn openly or leave the tent. The LORD tells Aaron that priests must not drink wine on duty. They must tell holy from common and teach Israel the laws. Moses is angry that the sin offering was burned, not eaten, and accepts Aaron’s answer.
events.detail: Aaron has lost two sons that day and may not mourn (verses 6–7). The rule was that priests eat the sin offering (6:26). Aaron’s remaining sons burned it, and Moses is angry (verses 16–18). Aaron answers with a question in verse 19. After “such things as these,” would eating it have pleased the LORD? He does not claim a rule; he asks what fits the day. Verse 20 says Moses was satisfied, and the chapter ends there.
events.uncertainty: The marker represents the traditional Sinai region. Leviticus gives no chapter-by-chapter travel route.

lds.text: The Church manual discusses responsibility in sacred service. Aaron explains why he did not eat the offering (verse 19). How does Moses respond in verse 20?

events.title: Animals and food
events.summary: The LORD tells Moses and Aaron which animals Israel may eat. Land animals must have a split hoof and chew the cud. Camels, hyraxes, hares, and pigs are unclean. Water creatures must have fins and scales. Many named birds are forbidden, and so are most winged insects, except locusts and grasshoppers. Touching a dead unclean animal makes a person unclean until evening. Pots and ovens that touch a carcass must be washed or broken. Israel must be holy, because the LORD who brought them from Egypt is holy.
events.detail: Verse 40 is about an animal Israel may eat that dies by itself. Someone has to move the body. The verse does not forbid it or call it sin. It says to wash clothes and wait until evening. So “unclean” here is a short state with a simple way out. It limits contact with holy things for a time. Verses 44–45 give the reason for the rules: “be holy; for I am holy.”
events.uncertainty: The marker represents the traditional Sinai region. Leviticus gives no chapter-by-chapter travel route.

lds.text: The Church manual studies these rules within Israel’s covenant. A person who carries a carcass is unclean “until the evening” (verse 40). What must that person do?

events.title: After childbirth
events.summary: A woman who bears a son is unclean for seven days. The boy is circumcised on the eighth day. She then waits thirty-three more days and may not enter the sanctuary. For a daughter the times are doubled: two weeks and sixty-six days. When the time ends, she brings the priest a lamb and a pigeon or dove. If she cannot afford a lamb, she brings two doves or two pigeons. The priest makes atonement for her, and she is clean.
events.detail: The chapter does not say the mother did wrong. Genesis 1:28 commands people to be fruitful. Her state comes from the blood of birth, as verses 4 and 7 say. It keeps her from holy things and the sanctuary for a set time. Verse 8 lowers the cost for a poor family, as 5:7 did. The result is the same either way: “she shall be clean.” Luke 2:22–24 reports that Mary brought the two birds.
events.uncertainty: The marker represents the traditional Sinai region. Leviticus gives no chapter-by-chapter travel route.

lds.text: A mother who cannot afford a lamb may bring two birds (verse 8). What result does the verse promise her?

events.title: Inspection of skin and cloth
events.summary: A person with a swelling, scab, or bright spot goes to a priest. The priest looks for white hair and a mark deeper than the skin. If it is unclear, he isolates the person for seven days and looks again. He may wait seven more days before deciding. A faded mark means clean, and a spreading one means unclean. A person with leprosy wears torn clothes, calls out “Unclean,” and lives outside the camp. Cloth or leather with a greenish or reddish spot is also shown to the priest. It is shut away seven days and burned if the spot spreads.
events.detail: The priest here works as an inspector, and the chapter gives him tests. He checks hair color, depth, and spread (verses 3–8). When the signs are unclear, verse 4 orders a seven-day wait. Verse 5 orders a second look and, if needed, a second wait. So no one is sent out of the camp on a first glance. Verse 46 shows why care matters: the unclean person must live alone outside.
events.uncertainty: The marker represents the traditional Sinai region. Leviticus gives no chapter-by-chapter travel route.

lds.text: The priest waits seven days, then seven more, before he decides (verses 4–5). How can a community care for people who must stay apart?

events.title: Return after cleansing
events.summary: This is the law for a healed leper. The priest goes outside the camp to examine him. Two birds are used: one is killed, and the living one is set free. The person washes, shaves, and waits seven days before entering his tent. On the eighth day he brings lambs, flour, and oil, and the priest makes atonement. A poor person may bring one lamb and two birds. A house with spreading mildew is emptied, shut up, scraped, and, if needed, torn down. A house that stays clear is declared clean.
events.detail: Chapter 13 sent the sick person outside the camp. Chapter 14 is about the way back. The priest goes out to meet him (verse 3). The return happens in steps: outside, into the camp, into the tent, to the altar. Verse 21 makes sure cost does not block the last step. A poor person brings one lamb, not three, and two birds. The closing words are the same for rich and poor: “he shall be clean.”
events.uncertainty: The marker represents the traditional Sinai region. Leviticus gives no chapter-by-chapter travel route.

lds.text: A poor person brings “such as he is able to afford” (verse 22). How does the chapter help someone return to the community?

events.title: Bodily discharges
events.summary: A man with a bodily discharge is unclean. His bed, his seat, and anyone he touches become unclean until evening. When it stops, he counts seven days, washes, and brings two birds to the priest. A man with an emission of semen bathes and is unclean until evening. A woman in her monthly period is unclean for seven days. A longer flow of blood makes her unclean for as long as it lasts. When it stops, she counts seven days and brings two birds. These rules keep Israel from defiling the tabernacle that is among them.
events.detail: The chapter covers things that happen to healthy bodies and to sick ones. It treats men first (verses 2–18) and women second (verses 19–30). Most cases need only washing and waiting until evening. None is called a crime. Verse 31 gives the reason for all of it: God’s tabernacle is “among them.” Because he lives in the camp, the people’s bodily states matter near his tent. The rules manage access to that tent and say nothing about a person’s worth.
events.uncertainty: The marker represents the traditional Sinai region. Leviticus gives no chapter-by-chapter travel route.

lds.text: Verse 31 gives the reason for these rules. What is it?

events.title: The Day of Atonement
events.summary: Aaron may not enter the Most Holy Place at just any time. Once a year he bathes and dresses in plain linen. He offers a bull for himself and his house. He casts lots over two goats: one for the LORD and one as the scapegoat. He takes incense and blood inside the veil and sprinkles the mercy seat. He makes atonement for the Holy Place, the tent, and the altar. He confesses Israel’s sins over the live goat and sends it into the wilderness. On that day, the tenth of the seventh month, all Israel rests and humbles itself.
events.detail: Verse 16 says atonement is made “for the Holy Place.” The reason is the people’s uncleanness and all their sins. The tent stands in the middle of the camp, so their wrongs reach it. Once a year the room, the tent, and the altar are cleansed (verse 20). Then the people’s sins are confessed over a goat and carried away (verses 21–22). The day clears both the place and the people. Verse 30 states the result: “You shall be clean from all your sins.”
events.uncertainty: The marker represents the traditional Sinai region. Leviticus gives no chapter-by-chapter travel route.

lds.text: The older Church manual connects the Day of Atonement with Christ’s work to forgive sin. Verse 16 says the tent dwells “in the middle of their uncleanness.” What is cleansed on this day besides the people?

events.title: Blood and the place of offering
events.summary: Anyone who kills a bull, lamb, or goat must bring it to the tent door. Killing it elsewhere counts as bloodshed. The rule is meant to end sacrifices in the open field to goat idols. The priest sprinkles the blood on the LORD’s altar. No Israelite or foreigner living among them may eat blood. The life is in the blood, and God gave it for atonement on the altar. A hunter must pour out the blood of his catch and cover it with dust. Anyone who eats an animal found dead must wash and wait until evening.
events.detail: The ban on eating blood appeared in Genesis 9:4 and Leviticus 3:17. Verse 11 is where the reason is given. Blood stands for the animal’s life. God says he has “given it to you on the altar” for atonement. So blood has one proper use, and it is not food. Verse 13 applies this even to wild game that is never offered. The hunter pours the blood out and covers it, treating the life with respect.
events.uncertainty: The marker represents the traditional Sinai region. Leviticus gives no chapter-by-chapter travel route.

lds.text: Verse 11 says “the life of the flesh is in the blood.” What must a hunter do with an animal’s blood in verse 13?

events.title: Limits on sexual conduct
events.summary: The LORD tells Israel not to follow the practices of Egypt or Canaan. They must keep his statutes and live by them. The chapter forbids sexual relations with close relatives, and it lists them one by one. It forbids marrying a wife’s sister as a rival, and adultery. It forbids giving children to Molech. It forbids a man lying with a man, and sex with animals. The nations before Israel did these things, and the land was defiled. The land vomited them out, and it will do the same to Israel.
events.detail: Most of the chapter concerns people who live in one large household. Verses 6–18 name mothers, sisters, granddaughters, aunts, and daughters-in-law. Each rule is addressed to the one who would approach, so the relative is protected. Verses 24–25 widen the view to the land itself. Canaan’s people defiled it, and it “vomited out her inhabitants.” Verse 28 gives Israel the same warning, with no special protection.
events.uncertainty: The marker represents the traditional Sinai region. Leviticus gives no chapter-by-chapter travel route.

lds.text: Verse 28 warns that the land can “vomit you out also.” Whom do the rules in verses 6–18 protect inside a household?

events.title: Holiness in daily life
events.summary: The LORD tells all Israel to be holy, because he is holy. They must respect parents, keep Sabbaths, and avoid idols. Farmers must leave field corners and fallen grapes for the poor and the foreigner. They must not steal, lie, hold back wages overnight, or trip the blind. Judges must not favor the poor or the great. They must not hate or take revenge, but love their neighbor as themselves. They must love the foreigner as themselves, since they were foreigners in Egypt. Scales, weights, and measures must be honest.
events.detail: The chapter opens with “You shall be holy” (verse 2). It then spends most of its length on fields, wages, courts, and trade. Verse 36 ends the list at the scale: just balances, weights, and measures. A false weight cheats a buyer; the trade weight shown is that kind of tool. The verse ends with the exodus: “who brought you out of the land of Egypt.” So honest trade is part of belonging to the God who freed them. The same chapter holds “love your neighbor as yourself” (verse 18).
events.uncertainty: The marker represents the traditional Sinai region. Leviticus gives no chapter-by-chapter travel route.

lds.text: How can love change the way you treat workers and strangers? Verse 36 requires honest weights. What does verse 13 require for a hired worker’s pay?

events.title: Penalties and distinction
events.summary: Anyone who gives a child to Molech must be stoned. If the people look away, God will act against that family. Those who turn to mediums are cut off. Israel must be holy and keep God’s statutes. Death is set for cursing parents, adultery, and several unions forbidden in chapter 18. Other unions bring being cut off or dying childless. Israel must not follow the customs of the nations being driven out. The LORD has set them apart to be his and to inherit the land.
events.detail: Chapter 18 listed forbidden acts. Chapter 20 attaches penalties, and many are death. Verses 2–5 begin with child sacrifice to Molech and blame neighbors who look away. Verses 22–23 give the reason: other nations did these things and lost the land. Verse 24 sets the promise beside the threat. Israel will inherit a good land and has been separated from the peoples. Verse 26 says what the separation is for: “that you should be mine.”
events.uncertainty: The marker represents the traditional Sinai region. Leviticus gives no chapter-by-chapter travel route.

lds.text: Consider moral responsibility while keeping ancient civil penalties distinct from present Church practice. The LORD says he has “separated you from the peoples” (verse 24). What promise comes with that in the same verse?

events.title: Rules for priests
events.summary: Priests may not touch the dead, except for their closest relatives. They may not shave their heads or cut their flesh. They may not marry a prostitute or a divorced woman. The high priest may not go near any dead body, even a parent’s. He must marry a virgin of his own people. A priest with a bodily defect may not come near the altar or the veil. The list includes the blind, the lame, and the injured. He may still eat the holy and most holy food.
events.detail: Verses 17–21 bar a priest with a bodily defect from offering at the altar. The same standard was set for the animals offered there (1:3). Verse 22 follows at once with what he keeps. He eats “the bread of his God,” both the holy and the most holy. That food was the priests’ living (6:16–18). So the limit is on one task, not on his place among the priests. The text does not call him unclean or sinful.
events.uncertainty: The marker represents the traditional Sinai region. Leviticus gives no chapter-by-chapter travel route.

lds.text: What duties come with service in a holy place? A priest with a defect may not serve at the altar (verse 21). What does verse 22 still give him?

events.title: Holy gifts and acceptable offerings
events.summary: Priests must stay away from the holy food while they are unclean. An unclean priest washes, waits until evening, and then may eat his bread. Only the priest’s household may eat it, including a slave he bought. A married daughter may not, but a childless widow who returns home may. Anyone who eats it by mistake repays it and adds a fifth. Animals for vows and free gifts must have no defect. A newborn animal stays seven days with its mother. A cow or ewe and its young may not be killed on the same day.
events.detail: Most of this chapter is about what makes an offering acceptable. Verses 27–28 add two limits that concern the animals themselves. A newborn stays with its mother for seven days. A mother and her young are not killed on the same day. The text gives no reason. The effect is to keep mother and young in view. Even at the altar, the animal’s life is given some regard.
events.uncertainty: The marker represents the traditional Sinai region. Leviticus gives no chapter-by-chapter travel route.

lds.text: An animal and its young may not be killed on one day (verse 28). What does verse 27 require for a newborn animal?

events.title: The sacred calendar
events.summary: The LORD gives Moses the set feasts of the year. The Sabbath comes every seventh day. Passover falls in the first month, with seven days of unleavened bread. A sheaf of first grain is waved, and fifty days later two loaves are offered. At harvest the field corners and gleanings are left for the poor and the foreigner. The seventh month has a day of trumpets and the day of atonement. Then comes the seven-day feast of booths. Israel lives in shelters to remember the journey out of Egypt.
events.detail: Verses 4–21 and 23–44 are a calendar of feasts and offerings. Verse 22 interrupts it with a rule about reaping. It comes right after the harvest feast of verses 15–21. The farmer who brings loaves to God must leave grain in the field. The poor and the foreigner have no harvest of their own to celebrate. The rule repeats 19:9–10 almost word for word. So the feast is not complete if the harvest is kept only for the owner.
events.uncertainty: The marker represents the traditional Sinai region. Leviticus gives no chapter-by-chapter travel route.

lds.text: A harvest rule sits in the middle of the feast list (verse 22). Whom does it provide for?

events.title: Lamps, bread, and a judgment
events.summary: Israel must bring pure olive oil so the lamp burns every night. Twelve loaves are set on the gold table each Sabbath, and the priests eat them. Then a fight breaks out in the camp. A man with an Israelite mother and an Egyptian father curses the Name. He is held until the LORD’s will is known. The LORD orders the hearers to lay hands on him and all to stone him. The LORD adds rules: life for life, eye for eye, and payment for animals. The same law applies to the foreigner and the native-born.
events.detail: The man in this case has an Egyptian father (verse 10). The people wait for the LORD’s word before acting (verse 12). The ruling does not rest on his mixed family. Verse 16 says a foreigner or a native-born person gets the same penalty. Verse 22 states it as a rule: “one kind of law” for both. The same verses limit payback to the harm done: eye for eye, no more. The sentence is severe, and the text reports that it was carried out (verse 23).
events.uncertainty: The marker represents the traditional Sinai region. Leviticus gives no chapter-by-chapter travel route.

lds.text: How can our words honor God? Verse 22 says one law covers the foreigner and the native-born. Why does that matter in this case (verses 10–11)?

events.title: Sabbath years and Jubilee
events.summary: Every seventh year the land must rest, with no sowing or pruning. After forty-nine years a trumpet announces the fiftieth year, the Jubilee. Liberty is declared, and each person returns to his family’s land. Land prices follow the number of crops left before the Jubilee. The land may not be sold forever, because it belongs to the LORD. A relative may buy back land for a poor brother. Israel must lend to the poor without interest. A poor Israelite who sells himself serves as hired help until the Jubilee.
events.detail: Verse 23 gives the reason behind the whole chapter. The land belongs to the LORD, and Israel lives on it as his guests. So a sale is really a lease of crops until the Jubilee (verses 15–16). A family that falls into debt gets its field back in the fiftieth year. Verse 42 says the same of people: Israelites are God’s servants, not slaves. The chapter does not extend that rule to foreigners (verses 44–46). Its limit on wealth protects Israel’s own families from permanent loss.
events.uncertainty: The marker represents the traditional Sinai region. Leviticus gives no chapter-by-chapter travel route.

lds.text: The LORD says, “The land is mine” (verse 23). What does that mean for a family that had to sell its field?

events.title: Covenant promises and warnings
events.summary: Israel must make no idols and must keep the Sabbaths. If they obey, God will send rain, harvests, peace, and victory. He will set his tent among them and walk with them. If they refuse, he will send sickness, defeat, drought, wild animals, and siege. Each stage is harder than the last. In the end their cities fall, and they are scattered among the nations. Then the land will enjoy the Sabbaths it missed. If they confess, God will remember his covenant with Jacob, Isaac, and Abraham.
events.detail: The warnings come in five stages (verses 16, 18, 21, 23, 27). Each stage is a chance to turn back before the next. The last stage is exile in an enemy’s land. Verse 44 begins “Yet for all that.” Even there God will not destroy them utterly or break his covenant. The reason given is his name: “for I am the LORD their God.” Verses 40–42 say what opens the way back: confession and a humbled heart.
events.uncertainty: The marker represents the traditional Sinai region. Leviticus gives no chapter-by-chapter travel route.

lds.text: What hope remains after the warnings? In verse 44 God says he will not reject his people in exile. What will he remember in verse 45?

events.title: Vows and dedicated property
events.summary: A person vowed to the LORD is given a value in silver. The value depends on age and sex, from three to fifty shekels. A poor person is valued by the priest according to what he can pay. An animal given for offering becomes holy and may not be swapped. A house or field may be dedicated and bought back by adding a fifth. A field’s value is counted by the years left until the Jubilee. Firstborn animals already belong to the LORD. A tenth of crops and herds is holy to the LORD.
events.detail: Verses 3–7 set fixed values for people who have been vowed. A fixed scale is simple, but it can be out of reach. Verse 8 handles that case. The priest sets a value “according to his ability to pay.” So a vow made in faith does not become a debt that crushes. The same care appeared in 5:7, 12:8, and 14:21. Leviticus ends as it began, making room for people with less.

lds.text: A person too poor for the set value goes to the priest (verse 8). How does the priest decide the amount?

guides.title: Leviticus: context and evidence
guides.description: Explore the book’s larger concerns through selected passages and relevant evidence.

steps.title: Access to worship includes those with less
steps.text: Verse 6 sets the normal offering at a lamb or goat. Verse 7 opens a second door for someone who “can’t afford a lamb.” Verse 11 opens a third: a small measure of flour. Each level ends with the same words: atonement, and “he will be forgiven.” So the price changes with the person’s means, and the result does not. Verse 5 asks one thing of everyone first: to confess. Verse 16 adds repayment plus a fifth where something was taken.

steps.title: Holiness reaches the marketplace
steps.text: The chapter opens with “You shall be holy” (verse 2). It then spends most of its length on fields, wages, courts, and trade. Verse 36 ends the list at the scale: just balances, weights, and measures. A false weight cheats a buyer; the trade weight shown is that kind of tool. The verse ends with the exodus: “who brought you out of the land of Egypt.” So honest trade is part of belonging to the God who freed them. The same chapter holds “love your neighbor as yourself” (verse 18).

steps.title: Land ownership has limits
steps.text: Verse 23 gives the reason behind the whole chapter. The land belongs to the LORD, and Israel lives on it as his guests. So a sale is really a lease of crops until the Jubilee (verses 15–16). A family that falls into debt gets its field back in the fiftieth year. Verse 42 says the same of people: Israelites are God’s servants, not slaves. The chapter does not extend that rule to foreigners (verses 44–46). Its limit on wealth protects Israel’s own families from permanent loss.
